"Rhapsody on the Great Man"
Xiàng Rú was appointed as the magistrate of the garden of Emperor Xiàowén;
seeing that the emperor favored immortals,
he then presented "Rhapsody on the Great Man."
Its words say:
There exists a great man,
located in the central region.
Whose dwelling spans myriad miles,
yet is still not enough for a brief stay.
Lamenting the narrow-mindedness of the world,
he abruptly takes flight for a distant journey.
Riding on scarlet banners and white rainbows,
carried by clouds and floating upwards.
I erect tall poles from the Gézé marsh,
Massing bright, shining pennants.
Hanging the first ten days of the month as a sash,
Trailing a comet as a tassel.
I wave the guiding bridge to make things incline,
And further wield the *yǐnǐ* to beckon and wave.
I grasp the *chānqiāng* stars as banners,
And unfurl a bent rainbow as a canopy.
Red obscurity blending with dark dimness,
A whirlwind rises, and clouds float.
I drive the *yìnglong* dragon-pulled carriage in sinuous beauty,
With red *chī* and blue *qiú* dragons as outriders, twisting and winding.
They bow and rise, bend and curl their skirts in arrogance,
Crooked and broken, bulging and cramped, leaping and prancing in connected coils.
Luxuriant and mighty, strong and forceful, standing still and mimicking,
Scattered and unrestrained, striding and neighing with shamefaced looks.
They step and pace, creak and pant, assuming postures of twisted beauty,
Cicada-like and coiled, inclining and bending, fearful and trembling, they lean and rely.
Entangled and agitated, shouting and arrogant, treading and stamping the path,
Covered and obscured, leaping and bounding, soaring and rushing wildly.
Rushing and rustling, flourishing and gathering, flaming and blazing, lightning flashing,
Suddenly, the mist clears,
Huòrán yún xiāo. Suddenly, the clouds dispersed.
Xié jué shǎoyáng ér dēng tàiyīn xī, Leaving behind the dying Shǎoyáng and ascending to Tàiyīn,
yǔ zhēnrén hū xiāng qiú. Seeking communion with the enlightened beings.
Hù zhé yǎotiǎo yǐ yòu zhuǎn xī, Repeatedly winding through secluded paths, turning to the right,
héng lì fēi quán yǐ zhèng dōng. Rushing swiftly across flowing springs, heading due east.
Xī zhēng líng yǔ ér xuǎn zhī xī, Gathering all the spirit guardians and selecting from them,
bùshǔ zhòng shén yú yáoguāng. Deploying the multitude of gods at Yáoguāng.
Shǐ wǔdì xiān dǎo xī, Ordering the Five Emperors to lead the way,
fǎn dà yī ér cóng língyáng. Returning to the Great One and following Língyáng.
Zuǒ xuánmíng ér yòu qiánléi xī, With Xuánmíng on the left and Qiánléi on the right,
qián chánglí ér hòu yùhuáng. Chánglí in front and Yùhuáng behind.
Sī zhēng Bó Qiáo ér yì Xiàn Mén xī, Employing Bó Qiáo in constant service and enlisting Xiàn Mén,
zhào Qí Bó shǐ Shàng Fāng. Summoning Qí Bó and sending Shàng Fāng.
Zhù Róng jǐng ér bì yù xī, Zhù Róng standing guard and clearing the way,
qīng qìfēn ér hòu xíng. Purifying the atmosphere before proceeding.
Tún yú chē ér wàn shèng xī, Gathering my chariots, a myriad of vehicles,
cuì yún gài ér shù huá qí. With plumed cloud canopies and raised ornate banners.
Shǐ Jù Máng qí jiāng xíng xī, Sending Jù Máng as my vanguard,
wú yù wǎng hū Nán'āi. I wish to travel to Nán'āi.
Lì Táng Yáo yú Chóngshān xī, Passing Táng Yáo at Chóngshān,
guò Yú Shùn yú Jiǔyí. Passing Yú Shùn at Jiǔyí.
Fēn zhànzhàn qí chācuò xī, The confused brilliance is chaotic,
zá tà jiāogé yǐ fāng chí. Mixed and abundant, wheels grinding, running in all directions.
Sāorǎo chōngcōng qí fēn ná xī, The disturbances rise up in confused agitation,
pāng bì yāng yà lì yǐ línlí. Abundant and abundant, the forest and the water mingle in disorder.
Cuán luóliè jù cóng yǐ lóngrōng xī, Massed together, spread out, clustered and in thick profusion,
Spreading out, flowing and glittering in a disorderly fashion.
Directly entering the thunder chamber with its booming and deep echoing sounds,
emerging from the ghost valley with its rugged and towering forms.
Widely surveying the eight cardinal points and observing the four seas,
swiftly crossing the Nine Rivers and traversing the Five Rivers.
Managing the flaming fire and floating on the weak water,
crossing the floating islands and wading through the shifting sands.
I took a rest, reaching the furthest extent, roaming the vast water regions,
ordering the divine Wā to play the zither and Féng Yí to dance.
When the times seemed to become dark and turbid,
I summoned Píng Yì to execute Fēng Bó,
and punish Yǔ Shī.
Looking westward towards the looming and indistinct Kūnlún,
I drove directly to the Sān Wēi mountains.
Pushing open the Chāng Hé gate and entering the Emperor's palace,
I carried jade maidens back with me.
Ascending Lángfēng mountain and gathering far away,
the lofty bird soared and stopped only once.
Lingering by the shadowy Yīn Shān, soaring with winding curves,
it was only today that I saw the Xī Wángmǔ.
With a bright white head, wearing a headdress and dwelling in a cave,
she was also fortunate to have a three-legged crow to serve as her messenger.
If one must live long like this and never die,
even living for ten thousand generations would not be enough to make one happy.
Turning the chariot and coming back quickly,
cutting through the path of Bù Zhōu,
and meeting for a meal in Yōu Dū.
Breathing in the mists and dews, I feast on the morning glow,
Chewing and savoring the essence of Ganoderma, I nibble at the splendid jades.
With caution I seek and ascend loftily,
The abundant clouds melt and rise keenly.
Piercing through the inverted image of the lightning,
I wade through the torrential downpour of Féng Lóng.
I gallop along the path and descend at length,
I rush past the lingering mists and vanish afar.
Pressed by the narrowness of the mundane world,
I stretch my joints and emerge from the northern edge.
Leaving behind the garrisoned cavalry at the dark palace,
Outstripping the vanguard at the cold gate.
Below, it is rugged and without ground,
Above, it is vast and without sky.
My sight is blurred and without vision,
My hearing is wide open and without sound.
Riding on emptiness, I ascend far away,
Surpassing all companions, I exist alone.

Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's (司馬相如)
"Běi Rén Fù" (美人賦) ("Rhapsody on a Beautiful Woman")
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, being handsome and leisurely,
traveled to the court of the King of Liáng.
The King of Liáng was pleased with him.
Zōu Yáng (鄒陽) slandered him to the King, saying:
"Xiàngrú is beautiful indeed,
but his attire and appearance,
are seductively unfaithful,
he intends to use flattering words to gain favor,
and roam the King's harem,
Has the King not noticed this?"
The King asked Xiàngrú, saying:
"Do you like women?"
Xiàngrú said:
"Your subject does not like women."
The King said:
"If you do not like women,
how are you like Kǒngzǐ and Mòzǐ?"
Xiàng Rú 相如 said,
"The ancients avoided beautiful women.
The followers of Kǒng 孔 and Mò 墨, upon hearing that Qí 齊 was offering women, went far away;
upon seeing Cháogē 朝歌, turned their carriages around,
like avoiding fire and water,
and seeking refuge from drowning in the mountain corners.
This is because they had not yet seen what was desirable.
How can this prove that they did not enjoy beautiful women?
As for your subject,
having grown up in the western lands,
and living alone in widowhood,
my house is vast and empty,
with no one to share my joy.
There is a woman to the east of my house,
with cloud-like hair, luxuriant and beautiful,
moth eyebrows and bright teeth,
her face flourishing, her color abundant,
her aura shining, her light rising.
She is always looking west,
wanting to stay with me and share my lodging.
She climbs the wall to look at me,
For three years now,
your servant has been rejected and not permitted to serve.
I secretly admired the great king's noble righteousness,
and ordered my carriage eastward.
On the way, I passed through Zhèng and Wèi,
and the road went through Sāngzhōng.
In the morning, I departed from Qín and Wěi,
and in the evening, I lodged at Shànggōng.
The secluded pavilion of Shànggōng,
was quiet, lonely, and empty.
Its doors were closed in the daytime,
dimly lit, as if a god resided there.
Your servant pushed open its door and entered its hall,
where a fragrant aroma was intense,
and embroidered curtains hung high.
A woman was alone,
elegantly seated on a bed,
her extraordinary beauty unrestrained,
her virtuous nature radiant and glorious.
Seeing me lingering,
she smiled and said:
"What country's noble son are you, honored guest?
From where you come, is it not far?"
Then she prepared fine wine
and presented a zither.
I then touched the strings
and played the tunes of "Yōulán" and "Báixuě."
The woman then sang:
"Alone in my chamber, I feel utterly desolate;
Thinking of my fair one, my heart is filled with sorrow.
O beautiful woman, why are you so late in arriving?
The day is already late, and beauty's colors fade;
How dare I entrust myself to one who is forever selfish?"
A jade hairpin hangs from my crown,
Silken sleeves brush against my robe.
The time is late evening,
Dark Yin is obscure and dim.
The flowing wind is bitter and cold,
White snow flutters and falls.
The secluded room is silent and still,
No human voice is heard.
Thereupon, bedding is arranged,
And precious ornaments and playthings are set out.
Golden censers emit fragrant smoke,
Embroidered curtains hang low,
Padded mattresses are layered,
Horn pillows are placed horizontally.
The woman then loosens her outer garments,
Revealing her inner clothing.
Her fair body is exposed,
With delicate bones and full flesh,
She comes to caress me,
Her softness like ointment.
I then steady my pulse within,
And rectify my heart within my breast,
Vowing faithfully,
"Bǐng zhì bù huí, fān rán gāo jǔ, yǔ bǐ cháng cí."

*Cháng Mén Fù*.
During the time of Empress Chén of Emperor Xiào Wǔ, she was favored,
and was quite jealous.
Separated in Cháng Mén Palace,
she was sorrowful and full of grieving thoughts.
She heard that Sīmǎ Xiàngrú of Chéngdū, Shǔ Commandery, was the most skilled writer in the world,
so she offered one hundred *jīn* of gold for Xiàngrú and Wénjūn to buy wine,
hoping for a composition to dispel her sorrow.
Then Xiàngrú wrote a text to enlighten the sovereign,
and Empress Chén regained the emperor's favor.
The text says:
"Ah, what a beautiful woman,
pacing leisurely to amuse herself.
Her soul wanders away and does not return,
her body withers and lives alone.
She says I go in the morning and return in the evening,
enjoying food and drink, forgetting people's hearts.
She is resentful, moving on and not remembering the past,
becoming intimate with those who are successful.
Alas, I am so slow and foolish,
Cherishing a joyful heart of sincerity and honesty.
Wishing for your inquiry and thus advancing myself,
hoping to receive the beautiful sound of your voice, my lord.
Offering empty words and hoping for sincerity,
anticipating the Lígōng 離宮 palace south of the city.
Preparing meager provisions and arranging them myself,
yet you, my lord, would not deign to grace me with your presence.
I live in solitude, deeply immersed in devotion,
while the heavens are vast and a fierce wind blows.
Ascending the Lántái 蘭臺 terrace and gazing into the distance,
my spirit wanders, feeling lost and disoriented.
Floating clouds gather and enclose all around,
the sky is deep and dark, and it is daytime yet gloomy.
Thunder rumbles and resounds,
its sound resembling the sounds of your carriage, my lord.
A swirling wind rises from the boudoir,
lifting the curtains of the bedchamber.
Cassia trees intertwine and mingle together,
their fragrance is intensely rich and sweet.
Peacocks gather and keep each other company,
black monkeys howl and sing at length.
Kingfishers flap their wings and flock together,
while luan and phoenix birds soar north and south.
My heart sighs, unable to find relief,
evil influences grow strong and attack within.
Descending the Lántái 蘭臺 terrace and strolling around,
I walk leisurely in the deep palace.
The main hall is massive, as if to create heaven,
rising densely and towering high.
Leisurely wandering in the east wing,
I gaze upon the boundless magnificence.
Pushing the jade doors, shaking the metal knockers,
the resounding noise is like the sound of bells.
Carving magnolias to make rafters,
and decorating the beams with ornamented apricots.
Displaying lush, meandering trees,
separating the storied pavilions and Chinese parasol trees that support each other.
Applying precious wood for the brackets,
piling up unevenly to support the beams.
At times, resembling a collection of similar objects,
like accumulated rocks about to fall.
Five colors dazzle and illuminate each other,
sparkling and radiant, creating light.
Finely arranging tiled bricks of intricate stone,
resembling the patterns of hawksbill turtle shells.
Hanging silk gauze curtains,
suspending linked cords of fine silk tassels.
Gently stroking the pillars and lintels in leisure,
surveying the curved terraces in their grandeur.
White cranes cry out with mournful wails,
a solitary female perches on a withered willow.
As dusk falls and sight is lost,
sadly entrusting myself to the empty hall.
Suspending the bright moon to illuminate myself,
I depart into the clear night in the secluded chamber.
I take up the elegant qín to change the melody,
Playing sorrowful thoughts that cannot be prolonged.
I press the flowing zhǐ to turn it back,
The sound is delicate and wondrous, then rises again.
I thread and experience the meaning within the piece,
The sentiment is impassioned and self-elevating.
Those on the left and right are saddened and shed tears,
Their tears flow freely, crisscrossing.
They exhale with suppressed sighs and added sobs,
Their slippers shuffle as they rise and wander about.
They lift their long sleeves to cover themselves,
Counting the past days' misfortunes.
There is no face to be shown,
And so I give in to weary thoughts and go to bed.
I gather fragrant ruò to use as a pillow,
And spread out quán lán and zhǐ xiāng as a mat.
Suddenly, in slumber, I dream,
And my spirit feels as if you, my lord, are beside me.
I awaken with a start and see nothing,
My soul wanders about as if lost.
The many roosters crow, causing me sorrow,
I rise and look at the moon's pure light.
I observe the ranks of the many stars,
Bì and Mǎo emerge from the east.
I gaze at the thick haze in the courtyard,
As if the frost of late autumn has descended.
The night is long, as if a year,
My heart is heavy, and I cannot endure it any longer.
I lie listlessly and wait for dawn,
The desolate pavilion stands tall and becomes bright again.
I, a concubine, secretly grieve for myself,
And will not dare to forget this, as the years pass.

"Shàng Shū Jiàn Liè" (Memorial to the Throne Recommending Against Hunting)
Your minister has heard that among things of the same kind, there are those with extraordinary abilities.
Therefore, strength is attributed to Wū Huò,
swiftness is ascribed to Qìng Jì,
and bravery is expected of Bēn Yù.
In your minister's foolish opinion,
if such men truly exist,
so too should such beasts.
Now, Your Majesty enjoys scaling steep inclines
and shooting fierce beasts.
Should you suddenly encounter a beast of uncommon talent,
startling you from an unprepared position,
and encroaching upon the pure dust of your entourage,
The carriage cannot even turn around,
people have no time to display their skills.
Even if there were the skills of Wū Huò and Féng Méng,
their strength could not be used.
Dried trees and rotten stumps all become obstacles.
This is like Hú Yuè arising from under the axle,
and Qiāng Yí touching wheel hubs.
How can it not be dangerous!
Even with complete security and no worries,
this is still not something that the Son of Heaven should be near.
Moreover, to clear the road before traveling,
and gallop only after the middle of the road is cleared,
even then there are occasional accidents with bits and bridles.
How much more so to tread through the Artemisia and reeds,
and race through the mounds and graves,
enjoying the pleasure of encountering beasts ahead,
while inwardly having no thought of preserving oneself from danger.
Would the harm not be difficult to avoid!
To lightly regard the weight of ten thousand chariots as not being secure,
and take pleasure in venturing out on a path with one chance in ten thousand of danger,
Your servant humbly believes Your Majesty should not do this.
For the enlightened see afar before things have sprouted,
and the wise avoid danger before it has taken form.
Disaster is often hidden in the subtle and concealed,
and erupts from what people neglect.
Therefore, a common saying goes:
"A family with thousands in wealth,
does not sit beneath overhanging eaves."
This saying, though small,
can be used to understand great matters.
Your subject wishes that Your Majesty would pay attention and carefully consider it.

*Yù Bā Shǔ Xí* ("Proclamation to the People of Bā and Shǔ"):
Informing the governor of Bā and Shǔ:
The barbarians have been acting independently,
and have not been punished for a long time.
They often encroach upon our borders,
troubling our officers and gentlemen.
After Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you cared for the entire realm,
pacifying and gathering the Central States.
Then, mobilizing armies and sending out troops,
you campaigned against the Xióngnú in the north.
The *chányú* (ruler of the Xióngnú) was terrified,
bound his arms in surrender,
knelt and sued for peace.
Kāngjū and the Western Regions,
with multiple translations, presented tribute,
bowed their heads and came to offer gifts.
Shifting our troops eastward,
the Mǐnyuè killed each other.
You also sent condolences to Pānyú,
The Crown Prince entered the court.
The rulers of the Southern Barbarians (Nán Yí),
and the chiefs of the Western Bo (Xī Bó),
constantly presented tribute offerings,
not daring to be remiss or negligent,
stretching their necks and raising their heels,
eagerly desiring and admiring civilization and righteousness,
wishing to become subjects.
The distances were vast,
and the mountains and rivers deep and obstructive,
preventing them from coming on their own.
Those who did not submit have already been punished,
while those who did good have not yet been rewarded.
Therefore, I sent a Commandant (zhōng láng jiàng) to treat them as guests.
Sending five hundred men each from Ba (Bā) and Shu (Shǔ) to present gifts,
protecting the envoy, but not like that,
there was no military action,
or the calamity of fighting.
Now I hear that you are raising troops and enacting laws,
alarming the young,
and worrying the elders.
Furthermore, the commandery is presumptuously transporting grain,
none of which is Your Majesty's intention.
Those who were supposed to go either flee and escape or become bandits and are killed,
which is also not the conduct of a subject.
The soldiers of the border commanderies,
upon hearing the smoke signals and seeing the signal fires burn,
All grasped their bows and galloped,
carried weapons and ran,
their sweat flowed continuously,
fearing only to fall behind.
They faced the gleaming blades,
braved the flying arrows,
resolved not to turn back,
determined not to hesitate.
Every person held a furious heart,
as if avenging a private feud.
Is it that they enjoyed death and hated life,
that they were not common people,
and that they served a different lord than Bā Shǔ?
They planned deeply and considered afar,
were anxious about the nation's troubles,
and enjoyed fulfilling the duties of a subject.
Therefore, they received fiefs with conferred tallies,
and were granted noble rank by splitting the guī scepter,
their position was that of a marquis,
and they resided in the ranks of the eastern mansions.
In the end, they left behind a prominent reputation for posterity,
and passed down land to their children and grandchildren.
Their conduct was exceedingly loyal and reverent,
and their position was exceedingly peaceful and comfortable.
Their reputation spread to infinity,
and their meritorious achievements were recorded and did not perish.
Therefore, virtuous men and gentlemen
would spill their brains and marrow in the Central Plains,
Dew and moisture nourish the wild grass without refusing.
Now, when an envoy carrying tribute arrives in Nányí,
they immediately kill him themselves as a thief,
or they flee and escape, ultimately being executed,
their bodies die without a name,
and they are posthumously named "Utterly Foolish,"
bringing shame upon their parents,
and becoming a laughingstock to the world.
The difference in people's capacity and understanding is,
isn't it vast!
However, this is not solely the fault of the envoys themselves.
The teachings of fathers and elder brothers are not prioritized,
the guidance of younger brothers and sons is not careful,
they lack integrity and have little sense of shame,
and the customs are not kind and generous.
That they are subjected to punishment and execution,
is it not fitting!
Your Majesty is concerned about the envoys and officials behaving like that,
and grieves for the unfilial and foolish people behaving in this way.
Therefore, you have sent reliable messengers
to inform the common people about the matter of conscripting soldiers,
and to enumerate for them the crimes of disloyalty leading to death,
rebuking the village elders (sānlǎo) and those respectful to elders (xiàodì) for their failure to teach and instruct.
Now is the time for farming,
and we are heavily burdening the common people.
I have already personally seen the nearby counties,
but I fear that those people in remote valleys, streams, mountains, and marshes may not have heard completely.
When the official proclamation arrives,
urgently dispatch it to the counties and districts,
causing them all to understand His Majesty's intention.
Do not neglect this.

"Bào Zhuō Wénjūn Shū" (報卓文君書 - Reply to Zhuō Wénjūn's Letter)
Though the five flavors are sweet,
would you rather have rice and millet first?
Though the five colors are brilliant,
they do not overshadow coarse cloth.
In this green garment,
I shall hold your pot.
The Jǐn River has mandarin ducks,
The Hàn palace has trees.
Reciting your joyful singing,
makes me retrace my former steps,
I ought not allow you to waste your youth on me and feel sad about growing old.
"Dá Shèng Lǎn Wèn Zuò Fù" (荅盛擥問作賦 - Answering Shèng Lǎn's Question about Composing Rhyme-Prose)
Combining silk threads to create patterns,
arranging brocades and embroideries as substance,
one warp, one weft,
one note of Gōng, one note of Shāng,
these are the traces of composing rhyme-prose.
The heart of the *fù* writer,
encompasses the universe,
and surveys all manner of people.
This is something obtained from within,
and cannot be transmitted.

*Nán Shǔ Fùlǎo* (Refuting the Elders of Shu)
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty, seventy-eight years have passed.
Virtue has flourished over six generations.
Martial prowess is abundant and widespread,
and profound grace is extensive.
All living beings are soaked in it,
overflowing beyond the borders.
Thereupon, an envoy was ordered to campaign westward,
following the current and sweeping away (resistance).
Wherever the wind of (Hàn power) reached,
nothing failed to yield.
Consequently, the *Rǎn* and *Máng* tribes gave allegiance.
The *Zuò* were pacified and the *Qióng* preserved.
*Sī Yú* was conquered,
*Jǔ Bāo Pú* was taken,
and the road was connected back to *Huán*.
Turning eastward, preparing to report,
(the envoy) arrived in the capital of Shǔ.
Twenty-seven elders, officials, and learned gentlemen
solemnly came to call.
After the greetings,
Jìn said:
"I have heard that the principle of the Son of Heaven's relationship with the 夷狄 (Yídí, foreign tribes)
is merely to restrain them without severing ties.
Now, dismissing the soldiers from the three commanderies
and opening the road to Yèláng
has been going on for three years.
Yet, the work is not completed,
the soldiers are weary and exhausted,
and the common people are not provided for.
Now, we are further engaging with the Western 夷 (Yí, foreign tribes),
the strength of the people is depleted,
and I fear we cannot finish this undertaking.
This is also a burden on the envoys.
I am secretly worried about this for you all.
Moreover, the association of Qióng, Zuò, and the Western Bó with the Central Kingdom
has been going on for many years,
too many to count.
The benevolent have not come with virtue,
and the strong have not annexed with force.
I suspect it is perhaps not feasible!
Now, to diminish the people of Qí to appease the 夷狄 (Yídí, foreign tribes),
to impair what we rely on to engage in useless endeavors,
I, a rustic and ignorant person,
do not understand what is being done."
The envoy said:
"What are you talking about?
If it were as you say,
then the people of Shǔ would not have changed their customs,

I have heard that the ancient sage kings,
understanding that people cannot bear to part with their loved ones,
therefore established rituals.
Now, people transgress them.
It is for this reason that I wish to be buried naked,
to correct the ways of the world.
Indeed, extravagant burials truly provide no benefit to the dead,
yet common people compete to outdo each other,
wasting money and resources,
burying them to rot underground.
Some even bury today and exhume tomorrow,
how is this really different from exposing a corpse in the wilderness!
Furthermore, death
is the transformation of the end of life,
and the returning of things [to their origin].
The returning gets to arrive,
the transforming gets to change,
These things each return to their true nature.
Returning to true nature is obscure and silent,
without form or sound,
and thus aligns with the Way's essence.
Now, embellishing the exterior to impress the masses,
and elaborate burials that obstruct the true nature,
cause those returning (to the earth) to be unable to arrive,
and those transforming (into something new) to be unable to change.
This is to cause things to each lose their proper place.
Furthermore, I have heard it said that
the spirit (jīngshén)
is what belongs to Heaven;
the physical body (xínghái)
is what belongs to Earth.
The spirit separated from the body,
each returns to its true nature;
therefore, it is called a ghost (guǐ).
The meaning of the word "ghost" (guǐ) is "returning."
The corpse remains alone, a lifeless lump,
how could it possibly have consciousness?
To wrap it in silks and brocades,
and separate it with coffins and outer coffins,
the limbs bound and tied,
the mouth filled with jade and stones,
wishing to transform but unable to do so,
it becomes suppressed and a withered waxen thing.
After a thousand years,
the coffins and outer coffins decay and rot,
Then I can return to the soil,
and go to my true home.
Speaking from this,
what use is there in being a long-term guest?
In the past, when Emperor Yáo was buried,
a hollowed-out log was used as a coffin,
and kudzu vines were used as ties.
Its bottom piercing did not disturb the springs,
and its top did not leak out the stench of decay.
Therefore, the sage kings valued ease in life,
and ease in death and burial.
They did not expend effort on what was useless,
nor did they waste wealth on what was meaningless.
Now, spending wealth on lavish funerals,
with layers upon layers of partitions,
the dead do not know,
and the living do not benefit,
this is called a great delusion.
Alas!
I will not do this.
